questions.q: Why is Salesforce's multi-tenant architecture considered a distributed-systems problem?
options: Because each customer org runs on its own completely isolated physical server
Because many independent customer orgs share the same underlying infrastructure, creating a "noisy neighbor" risk that must be controlled
Because Salesforce does not use a network at all internally
Because multi-tenancy eliminates the need for any resource limits
questions.explain: Multi-tenancy means many customers share infrastructure, so one tenant's inefficient usage could degrade the experience for others unless the platform enforces limits — the same problem any distributed system with shared resources faces.

questions.q: Conceptually, what are Salesforce governor limits an example of?
options: Eventual consistency
Rate limiting / backpressure — a deliberate cap on resource usage per transaction to protect the shared platform
A consensus protocol like Raft
A message queue delivery guarantee
questions.explain: Governor limits cap things like SOQL queries and CPU time per transaction regardless of what a given transaction 'needs,' which is the rate-limiting concept applied to a multi-tenant platform.

questions.q: What do Platform Events implement on the Salesforce platform?
options: A synchronous, blocking request/response pattern
A publish/subscribe pattern — one event published once, consumed independently by multiple subscribers
A strongly consistent distributed database
A circuit breaker for governor limits
questions.explain: Platform Events let one event be published and then consumed independently by however many subscribers are listening, mirroring the pub/sub messaging pattern from earlier in the course.

questions.q: Why does this lesson avoid quoting specific governor limit numbers?
options: Because governor limits don't actually exist
Because the exact numeric limits change between Salesforce releases, while the underlying rate-limiting concept stays the same
Because numeric limits are a trade secret
Because governor limits only apply to sandbox orgs, never production
questions.explain: Salesforce revises specific limit values over time, so the lesson focuses on the durable concept (rate limiting to protect shared infrastructure) rather than numbers that could become outdated.

questions.q: What is the benefit of moving work to Queueable Apex or Batch Apex instead of running it synchronously?
options: It guarantees the work will run exactly once with no possibility of failure
It lets large or long-running work complete asynchronously without forcing the user to wait inside a single governor-limited transaction
It removes the need for governor limits entirely
It converts the operation into a strongly consistent one automatically
questions.explain: Asynchronous Apex mechanisms let work run outside the synchronous request path and across multiple transactions, so jobs that wouldn't fit in one limited transaction can still complete without blocking the user.
